methods.label: Method 1: Expand the possible quotient
methods.explanation:
A quadratic factor of a polynomial of degree at most three has a quotient of degree at most one. Thus, for constants \(u\) and \(v\), the factor condition gives
\[
ax^3+bx^2+1=(x^2-x-1)(ux+v).
\]
Allowing \(u=0\) also covers a possible lower-degree polynomial. Expanding the right side gives
\[
ux^3+(v-u)x^2-(u+v)x-v.
\]
Matching constant terms yields \(-v=1\), so \(v=-1\). The original polynomial has no \(x\) term, so \(u+v=0\), giving \(u=1\). Consequently, matching the \(x^2\) coefficients gives
\[
b=v-u=-1-1=-2.
\]
The cubic coefficient is \(a=u=1\). Both values are integers, and
\[
(x^2-x-1)(x-1)=x^3-2x^2+1
\]
verifies the required factorization. Thus \(b=-2\), choice A.
methods.levelReason: Degree reasoning, polynomial multiplication, and elementary coefficient equations are standard school algebra.

methods.label: Method 2: Find the remainder
methods.explanation:
A polynomial is divisible by \(D(x)=x^2-x-1\) exactly when its remainder on division by \(D\) is zero. To find that remainder, replace higher powers by linear expressions plus multiples of \(D\). We have
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2&=D(x)+x+1,\\
x^3&=(x+1)D(x)+2x+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second identity follows by multiplying the first by \(x\), then using the first again for the resulting \(x^2\). Thus the remainder of \(ax^3+bx^2+1\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(x)&=a(2x+1)+b(x+1)+1\\
&=(2a+b)x+(a+b+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
This has degree less than two, as a remainder must. It is the zero polynomial exactly when
\[
2a+b=0,\qquad a+b+1=0.
\]
Subtracting the second equation from the first gives \(a-1=0\), so \(a=1\) and \(b=-2\). These integer values make both remainder coefficients zero, so they satisfy the factor condition. Therefore \(b=-2\), choice A.
methods.levelReason: The remainder is derived through elementary polynomial identities, followed by solving two linear equations.
